:where() and :is() match identically, but :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument, while :where() always contributes zero. This makes :where() the right tool specifically for 'match this, but don't let it out-compete anything.'

Common mistake

Reaching for :is() when the goal is actually to LOWER specificity — :is() doesn't lower it, :where() does.

`:is()` takes on the specificity of its most specific argument, so the id inside it still counts — unlike `:where()`, which always contributes zero
`:is()` always contributes more specificity than the plain, unwrapped selector would
`:is()` is simply invalid syntax and would be ignored by the browser
items.explanation: `:is()` and `:where()` match identically, but `:is()` inherits the specificity of its most specific argument — the id inside it still counts. Only `:where()` is guaranteed to contribute zero, which is exactly why it (not `:is()`) is the tool for deliberately lowering specificity.
items.reflection: `:where()` lets you keep a selector matching the same elements while erasing its weight in the conflict it would otherwise win. Where else have you seen a tool that lets something keep acting/matching/qualifying without it also automatically gaining the authority that normally comes with it?

→ (0, 1, 0) — only .btn (outside :where()) counts

Why: :where()'s ENTIRE argument list contributes zero specificity, by spec.
